When chlorine gas was first used in 1915, soldiers had no protection; the first 'masks' were actually rags soaked in their own urine (the ammonia helped neutralize the chlorine). By the time of the film's setting, the 'Small Box Respirator' had been developed. It was a complex device made of rubber and glass with a charcoal filter. Failure to put the mask on within six seconds of a 'Gas!' warning meant permanent lung damage or a slow, excruciating death.
accuracyNote: The film's visual depiction of WWI equipment is exceptionally high, reflecting the industrialization of mass slaughter.

sources.title: Gas Masks in WWI (National WWI Museum)

mediaConnection: This card explores the survival equipment seen in Sam Mendes' '1917'.
mediaChanged: Media often treats them as accessories; history shows the claustrophobic panic and physical strain of wearing them for hours.
whyItMatters: The gas mask is the symbol of when war stopped being 'noble' and became a cold, industrial science.
quickRealityCheck: True. Gas mask technology saved millions of lives in the trenches.

title: The Wars of the Roses: The Real Westeros
subtitle: The bloody English history that inspired Game of Thrones
realHistory:
### The Dynasty Clash: York vs. Lancaster (Stark vs. Lannister)
The Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) was a series of dynastic civil wars for the throne of England between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster (Red Rose) and the House of York (White Rose). This is the primary historical blueprint for the Stark vs. Lannister conflict. The Yorks, much like the Starks, were seen as northern-aligned military men, while the Lancasters represented the southern, wealthier establishment. It was a 30-year game of musical chairs that decimated the English nobility.

### The 'Kingmaker': Warwick the Powerful
Westeros has Lord Varys and Littlefinger, but real history had Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick. Known as 'The Kingmaker,' he was the wealthiest and most powerful man in England. He could raise armies that rivaled the King's. He famously switched sides between York and Lancaster based on his personal interests, proving that in medieval politics, power wasn't just in the crown, but in the hands of the men who made kings. His eventual fall is a reminder that in the game of thrones, you win or you die.

### The Black Dinner: The Real Red Wedding
George R.R. Martin famously based the 'Red Wedding' on the 'Black Dinner' of 1440. In Scottish history, the young Earl of Douglas and his brother were invited to dinner with the King at Edinburgh Castle. During the meal, a black bull's head—the symbol of death—was brought in. The brothers were then dragged out and executed, violating the 'sacred law of hospitality.' This event shows that the most dangerous place in the Middle Ages wasn't the battlefield, but the dinner table.

### The Wall and Hadrian: The Northern Boundary
The massive ice wall in the North is inspired by Hadrian's Wall, which Martin visited in Northern England. Built by Emperor Hadrian in 122 AD, it marked the boundary of the Roman Empire against the 'barbarians' to the north. The feeling of isolation and the constant watch for an unknown threat from the wilderness is exactly what inspired the 'Night's Watch.'
accuracyNote: The series captures the ham-fisted brutality and shifting alliances of the era, though the 'Red Wedding' in history was even more politically complex than the show depicts.

mediaChanged: Martin added dragons and magic; history provided the even-more-shocking betrayals and the slow-motion collapse of a royal house.
whyItMatters: The Wars of the Roses shaped the modern English identity and led to the rise of the Tudor dynasty, which changed the world.
quickRealityCheck: True. Nearly every major 'shocker' in Game of Thrones has a more brutal real-history counterpart.

title: The Battle of the Bastards and Hastings
subtitle: Shield walls, arrow storms, and the piles of the dead
realHistory: The claustrophobic intensity of the 'Battle of the Bastards' is famously inspired by the Battle of Hastings in 1066. At Hastings, the Saxon King Harold formed a 'shield wall' on a ridge that the Norman cavalry couldn't break for hours. The piles of bodies grew so high that both sides struggled to move—a detail vividly captured when Jon Snow is nearly crushed by his own men. The battle ended when the shield wall finally broke, leading to a massacre that changed the course of English history.
accuracyNote: The show uses giants and fiction, but the 'shield wall' and the physical reality of a pre-modern slaughter are historically accurate.
mediaConnection: This card explores the tactical inspiration for the 'Battle of the Bastards'.
mediaChanged: The show focuses on the individual hero; history shows it was a clash of two rigid military cultures.
whyItMatters: Hastings is the reason the English language is a mix of Germanic and French today.
quickRealityCheck: True. 'Shield walls' were the absolute standard for survival in medieval warfare.

title: King Alfred and the Vision of England
subtitle: The Last Kingdom and the birth of a nation
realHistory: King Alfred 'the Great' was the only Saxon king to successfully defend his kingdom (Wessex) against the Viking Great Heathen Army. His victory at the Battle of Edington in 878 saved Anglo-Saxon culture. However, his true legacy wasn't just on the battlefield; it was his 'Burh' system (fortified towns) and his promotion of the English language over Latin. Alfred was the first to envision 'Englaland'—a unified nation of all Saxons. While he never ruled all of England, he laid the administrative and cultural foundation for his grandson, Athelstan, to become the first true King of all England.
accuracyNote: The series accurately portrays Alfred as a sickly but brilliant strategist, a depiction grounded in the contemporary biography by Asser.
mediaConnection: This card explores the historical figure of King Alfred in 'The Last Kingdom'.
mediaChanged: The show focuses on the Viking conflict; history emphasizes Alfred's role as a scholar and law-giver.
whyItMatters: Alfred is the reason England exists as a distinct cultural and linguistic entity today.
quickRealityCheck: True. Alfred was one of the few medieval kings who could actually read and write.

title: The Medieval Diet: Not Just Bread
subtitle: Kingdom Come: Deliverance and the reality of 1403
realHistory: In 1403 Bohemia, the diet was strictly defined by social class. For 90% of the population, the staple was 'pottage'—a thick vegetable and grain stew. Meat was a luxury, especially since forest game was the exclusive property of the lords. Interestingly, because water was often contaminated, people of all ages drank 'small ale' (low alcohol beer) throughout the day as their primary source of hydration. Potatoes, corn, and tomatoes were completely unknown, as they hadn't yet arrived from the Americas.
accuracyNote: Kingdom Come: Deliverance is celebrated for its accurate depiction of medieval food, including the specific herbs and grains of the era.
mediaConnection: This card explores the survival mechanics in 'Kingdom Come: Deliverance'.
mediaChanged: Media shows massive roasts; history shows that for most people, a good piece of bacon was a once-a-month celebration.
whyItMatters: The diet explains the physical health and economic constraints of the people who built the cathedrals.
quickRealityCheck: True. 'Pottage' was the fuel of the Middle Ages.

title: The Siege Reality: Hunger over Swords
subtitle: Why most castles were won without a fight
realHistory: In Total War, sieges are dramatic assaults with towers and rams. In reality, 90% of sieges were won by starvation. An army would simply surround a castle and wait. For the defenders, the greatest enemies were dysentery (from bad water) and hunger. For the attackers, the challenge was feeding thousands of soldiers in a single spot for months. Most castles didn't fall to a heroic breach, but to a bribe—a single guard opening a side gate for a loaf of bread or a bag of gold.
accuracyNote: The game focuses on the combat for fun, but the 'attrition' mechanic in the campaign map is a nod to this historical reality.
mediaConnection: This card explores the strategic reality behind 'Total War' sieges.
mediaChanged: Media focuses on the action; history shows that a siege was a long, boring, and disease-ridden endurance test.
whyItMatters: It reminds us that logisticians win wars, not just generals.
quickRealityCheck: True. Starvation was the most effective 'siege weapon' in history.

title: Medieval Diplomacy: Marriage and Blood
subtitle: Using family to secure a kingdom
realHistory: Medieval diplomacy wasn't just about treaties; it was about family. In the 11th-15th centuries, a princess was often a 'peace-weaver,' sent to a rival kingdom to cement an alliance. These marriages created a massive web of kinship that defined European borders. The Hundred Years' War, for example, was essentially a family dispute over inheritance. Ambassadors were not just messengers, but legal experts who spent months negotiating 'dowries'—which were often entire provinces or strategic castles.
accuracyNote: Total War: Medieval II captures this through its 'Princess' agent, whose primary job is to secure alliances through marriage.
mediaConnection: This card explores the political layer of 'Total War: Medieval II'.
mediaChanged: Games use a simple 'trust score'; history shows it was a complex legal and personal contract that could last for generations.
whyItMatters: It explains why modern European royalty is still so closely related today.
quickRealityCheck: True. In the Middle Ages, the King *was* the state, and his family was the state's primary asset.

title: A Day in Feudal Japan
subtitle: Peasants, monks, and the rice economy
realHistory: Over 90% of the population in Feudal Japan were peasants, and their lives revolved entirely around rice. Rice was not just food; it was the currency (Koku). A single 'Koku' was defined as the amount of rice one adult needed to survive for a year. Samurai were paid in rice, and the wealth of a Daimyo was measured by his land's rice production. While peasants paid high taxes, they often enjoyed significant local autonomy, managing their own village disputes as long as the quotas were met. Buddhist temples served as the community hubs—places of education, safety, and local governance.
accuracyNote: The series 'Shogun' accurately reflects the high value placed on rice and the strict social hierarchy that governed everyday interactions.
mediaConnection: This card provides the social context for the world of 'Shogun'.
mediaChanged: Media focuses on the samurai; history shows that the economic power of the peasant class was the true foundation of the Sengoku period.
whyItMatters: The rice economy explains why Japanese feudalism was so remarkably stable despite constant internal warfare.
quickRealityCheck: True. Rice was more important than gold in medieval Japan.

title: Samurai Warfare: Duel vs. Tactic
subtitle: Honorable standoffs and the Mongol collision
realHistory: Traditional 13th-century Japanese warfare was centered around individual 'Standoffs' (Meigen), where warriors would shout their lineage and challenge opponents to single combat. This changed forever during the Mongol invasions. The Mongols fought as a disciplined, collective unit using gunpowder bombs (Tetsuhau) and coordinated arrow storms directed by drums. The samurai were forced to adapt, moving away from individual duels toward fortified defenses and mounted archery. Interestingly, the 'Katana' didn't yet exist in its modern form; Jin Sakai would have likely used a 'Tachi,' a longer and more curved blade designed for cavalry.
accuracyNote: Ghost of Tsushima uses Jin's struggle to reflect the historical shift from traditional to pragmatic warfare, though it takes creative liberty with the weaponry.
mediaConnection: This card explores the historical shift seen in 'Ghost of Tsushima'.
mediaChanged: The game turns it into a personal moral choice; history shows it was a brutal necessity for national survival.
whyItMatters: This conflict gave birth to the 'Bushido' myth that later came to define the samurai identity.
quickRealityCheck: True. The Mongol invasion was the first time Japan faced a truly foreign military culture.

title: The Mongol Navy and the Divine Wind
subtitle: The moment the empire hit the sea
realHistory: Kublai Khan's invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281 featured some of the largest armadas in pre-modern history. However, the Mongols were a steppe people, not sailors. Their fleet was built by conscripted Chinese and Korean shipwrights. Archaeological underwater research has shown that the ships were built in a hurry, with poor rivets and weak joints. When a massive typhoon (the 'Kamikaze' or Divine Wind) hit in 1281, 80% of the fleet was destroyed. This confirmed the Japanese belief that their islands were protected by the gods and effectively ended the Mongol expansion into the Pacific.
accuracyNote: Ghost of Tsushima captures the arrival of the fleet, but the eventual destruction was more due to the sea than the samurai.
mediaConnection: This card explores the background of the invasion in 'Ghost of Tsushima'.
mediaChanged: In the game, the Mongols are nearly unstoppable; in reality, they were profoundly out of their element on the water.
whyItMatters: It marks one of the few total failures of the Mongol military machine.
quickRealityCheck: True. The 'Kamikaze' really did save Japan from Mongol rule.

title: The Real Assassins: Fedayeen of Alamut
subtitle: Beyond the white hoods: The Nizari Ismaili State
realHistory: The 'Assassins' of AC are a secret global order. In reality, they were a specific sect called the Nizari Ismailis, led by Hasan-i Sabbah from the mountain fortress of Alamut starting in 1090. Because they lacked a large army, they developed a doctrine of asymmetric warfare—using 'Fedayeen' (those who sacrifice themselves) to carry out high-profile assassinations of political rivals, like the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk. These agents were highly trained, often learning local languages and customs to infiltrate enemy courts for months before striking.
accuracyNote: While the game's 'Templar vs Assassin' conflict is fictional, the use of targeted assassination as a survival strategy is historically accurate.
mediaConnection: This card explores the real-world origin of the 'Assassin's Creed' series.
mediaChanged: The name 'Hashshashin' was likely a derogatory term used by their enemies to suggest they were drug-addled; there is no historical proof they used hashish.
whyItMatters: The Assassins invented a form of political warfare that changed the history of the Middle East.
quickRealityCheck: True. The word 'Assassin' enters English directly because of this 11th-century sect.

title: The Knights Templar: Rise and Execution
subtitle: From holy warriors to the first global bankers
realHistory: The Templars were founded in 1119 to protect pilgrims in the Holy Land. However, they soon became the wealthiest and most powerful military order in Europe. They created the first modern banking system, allowing travelers to deposit money in Paris and withdraw it in Jerusalem via letters of credit. This wealth eventually led to their doom; King Philip IV of France, who was deeply in debt to them, accused them of heresy in 1307. On Friday, October 13th, hundreds were arrested, and their Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was eventually burned at the stake in 1314.
accuracyNote: The game uses the Templars as a secret society; historically, they were a very public, Pope-sanctioned organization that was destroyed by the very state it served.
mediaConnection: This card explores the antagonists of 'Assassin's Creed'.
mediaChanged: While they remain a secret organization in games, in reality they were so powerful that they lent money to kings.
whyItMatters: The fall of the Templars is the ultimate warning of what happens when a financial power challenges a sovereign state.
quickRealityCheck: True. The Templars were the world's first truly 'too big to fail' institution.

title: Life in the Crusader Cities: Acre and Jerusalem
subtitle: The cosmopolitan reality of the 12th century
realHistory: In the first AC game, Acre and Jerusalem are tense war zones. Historically, they were also the most cosmopolitan cities in the world. Acre was a bustling trade hub where Venetian, Genoese, and Muslim traders operated side-by-side. Despite the warfare, cultural exchange was constant; the Crusaders adopted Eastern hygiene (hammams), medicines, and fashions, while Muslim officials often worked within the Crusader administrative systems. Jerusalem remained a spiritual magnet, with pilgrims of all faiths creating a linguistic and cultural melting pot in its streets.
accuracyNote: The game captures the architectural grandeur of these cities, though it emphasizes the tension over the daily commercial co-existence.
mediaConnection: This card provides the environmental context for the original 'Assassin's Creed'.
mediaChanged: Media shows constant battle; history shows that people still had to buy bread and trade spices even during a crusade.
whyItMatters: These cities were the first 'global hubs' where East and West truly learned about each other.
quickRealityCheck: True. Acre was the busiest port in the world for over a century.
